extracted.intended_audience: aspiring satirical/news-headline writers submitting to sites like Reductress, The Onion, The Hard Times, etc.
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical techniques for generating, editing, and submitting short, news-style satirical headlines to online satire venues; includes workforce habits, headline formulas, and notes on submission/trial processes for outlets like The Onion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit batches (headlines vs full pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to satirical news sites is a little different than other satire sites because you often submit batches of headlines rather than a full piece (and sometimes the sites only run a headline without a full article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare packets of multiple headlines for submission; expect some sites to publish only the headline. Target markets and their submission formats matter (some accept headline batches, others require trials or referrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorm continuously / write a bunch
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a bunch of headlines and brainstorm continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force a high volume of ideas so you hit the mindset where you 'refract every thought' through 'Could this be a headline?' — being in that zone makes ideas come naturally and increases chances of a publishable line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a real headline's first half as the setup and twist the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the source material for the thing you're making fun of, take the first half of a real headline, and use it as the setup, then fill in the end with a funny twist, which serves as the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimicking an authentic headline opening gives context and makes the twist land as satire. Use similar wording and tone for the setup so the reader expects a normal news line before the subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimic normal tone/wording for context, then break it with unexpected twist
rubrics_metrics.description: It's helpful to mimic the 'normal' thing (e.g., using similar wording, matching tone), because it sets up the context, then your funny, silly, imaginative idea breaks the context with something unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match syntax and cadence of genuine headlines to make the joke land as a news inversion. Anti-pattern: a headline that reads too opinionated or too obviously 'jokey' in the setup — the humor often works best when the setup feels legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep headlines short; shorten unnecessary syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: The shorter the better. That means sometimes taking out even syllables that feel unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the headline aloud; if you stumble or slow down, shorten it. Shortening improves punch timing and shareability. Edit ruthlessly to remove filler words that dilute the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit word choice and word order for rhythm and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fewer words, delete unnecessary articles (e.g., 'the'), place modifiers for clarity (e.g., 'people-pleasing woman' instead of 'woman who is people-pleasing'), and choose the single word that lands best (e.g., evaluating 'titties' vs 'boobs').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try multiple variants and prefer the phrasing that best preserves rhythm, brevity, and punch. Small word swaps can change tone (news-y vs opinion) and affect virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond the first idea — find another angle/layer
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to go beyond the first thing that comes to mind; spend time figuring out how to get at that joke from another angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first idea is often obvious; adding another layer or a news-like veneer can make it feel more like a headline and less like mere commentary. Brainstorm alternatives rather than settling on the immediate thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write daily practice volume (e.g., 10 jokes a day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 10 jokes a day. Not all of them will be news-style satire, and definitely not all will be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat headline-writing as a skill practiced by output. Daily quotas build idea muscle and provide raw material for later editing or submission packets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wait a few days before submitting (let the idea age-test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you want to submit a headline, WAIT a few days. I recommend waiting three days to see if it's still funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the idea survives time and still makes you laugh, it's more likely to work for others. Avoid impulsive submissions when enthusiasm is ephemeral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect editorial processes and high-volume rejection (Onion trial specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion's headline trial process: you may apply via careers, get recommended, or be invited to a trial; in a trial you might submit 10 headlines every Thursday into a pool that editors sift into a Shortlist and then a Roundup; many groups of 10 are unceremoniously rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know each outlet's process (open submissions vs referrals vs trials). Be prepared for low pay, impersonal selection, and the need for persistence. Use referral routes, workshops, or community groups to learn internal norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground the joke in topical/source material for news-feel
rubrics_metrics.description: Take inspiration from real news items (e.g., Hooters closing amid bankruptcy) and keep enough of the original headline to give context, then end with a funny twist to preserve a news-like feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping part of the factual hook makes the satire read like a plausible headline and helps the reader immediately understand the target. Anti-pattern: a headline with no recognizable news anchor can feel untethered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it simple and relatable to increase spread and spark debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, relatable headlines often spread quickly and can spark debate (e.g., a headline that is obvious or taps into common experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatability increases shareability and engagement. Don't overcomplicate the joke; aim for clarity so the audience connects instantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop many variants and iterate to the tightest version
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshopped multiple versions of a headline and ultimately chose the leanest phrasing; e.g., several variants were tried before deleting words and tightening the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate several rewrites, compare variants aloud, and choose the one that conveys context and punch with minimal words. Iteration often involves cutting, reordering, and swapping single words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the contextual portion brief so it doesn't steal the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the portion of the headline that's there for context so long that it's taking away from the joke? Shorten it!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context should set up the premise quickly; if it drags, the punch loses force. Trim context to the minimum needed for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw on personal moments or observations for authentic set-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal experiences and specific moments (e.g., overheard lines, lived situations) can generate strong headline ideas and provide a distinct, relatable angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture the exact moment/phrase and translate the specificity into the headline; authentic details often make satire feel sharper and more original.
